newsitem.title: LEBANON: Lebanon police snuff out protest during strike.
newsitem.headline: Lebanon police snuff out protest during strike.

text.p: Baton-wielding Lebanese police dispersed several hundred demonstrators trying to march in Beirut on Thursday during a general strike against the government of billionaire Prime Minister Rafik al-Hariri.

Security sources said 70 people were arrested during skirmishes in a city square and nearby backstreets in which roaming groups of demonstrators totalling up to 500 people shouted "Bread, Education, Freedom."
A few demonstrators shouted "Down with Hariri," a billionaire construction tycoon who has held office since October 1992.
The protest took place hours after Hariri won a resounding victory in parliament with a 102-19 vote of confidence for his new government.
Most of Beirut was semi-deserted as a general strike, called to protest "violations of freedom and democracy" by Hariri's government, cleared the capital's normally bustling streets.

The government flooded much of the city with soldiers and police to prevent the planned demonstration, but it held back from giving the army power to impose a curfew as it did when faced by similar strike and protest calls in February.
Security forces also snuffed out the attempted demonstration in Beirut easily and there were no attempts at similar protests in other cities.

The protests were called by opposition groups, labour unions, students and media workers against Hariri's perceived failure to improve social conditions during his rule and a decision to close scores of radio and television stations.
The opposition also demanded the lifting of a three-year-old ban Hariri has imposed on demonstrations, which they call illegal.
The government refused to lift the ban, but Hariri has promised to make social issues -- education, transportation, housing and employment -- a priority of his new government.

He also reached a last-minute compromise with parliament on Wednesday to postpone the shutdown of most of Lebanon's private radio and television stations to allow time for new applications for broadcasting licences to be considered. No date was given for the postponement.

The stations had been due to close by Saturday under a law regulating the audiovisual media. The opposition complain that all opposition stations have been refused licences in a deliberate attempt to muzzle the media.
They also say the decision to give broadcast licences mainly to stations owned or controlled by establishment figures like Hariri is a carve-up of the lucrative broadcasting industry.

Schools and most shops closed in the capital, but banks and many businesses opened and the stock exchange and financial markets carried on business as usual. Beirut airport was also virtually unaffected by the stoppage.

Outside Beirut, Reuters reporters said only schools closed in Tripoli and Baalbek, the main northern and eastern cities, and most shops opened by noon in the southern cities of Sidon and Tyre after staying closed during the morning.
